lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand the biological consequences of smoking in relation to the lungs and the circulatory system, including coronary heart disease

primer.text: Cigarette smoke is a chemical assault on two systems at once. Nicotine, carbon monoxide and tar each have a separate route of damage — vessels, blood chemistry and lung tissue — and the lung diseases they grow, chronic bronchitis and emphysema, dismantle the exchange surface itself.

modules.title: Three Chemicals, Three Attack Routes
modules.opening: Nicotine narrows blood vessels and speeds the heart, pushing blood pressure up and clot risk with it. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin irreversibly, shrinking the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and forcing the breathing and circulation to work harder. Tar is a carcinogen that also feeds chronic obstructive pulmonary disease — chronic bronchitis and emphysema together.
keyPoints: Nicotine narrows vessels, raises heart rate and blood pressure, and promotes clots.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin irreversibly, cutting oxygen capacity.
With less oxygen carried, breathing must quicken and deepen to compensate.
The heart pumps faster too, raising coronary heart disease and stroke risk.
Tar is a carcinogen and contributes to COPD: chronic bronchitis plus emphysema.

low.restatement: Each smoke chemical has its own target: vessels, blood cargo, or tissue.
low.analogy: Three intruders through one door — one jams the pipes, one steals the delivery vans, one burns the warehouse.
low.examPointer: Match chemical to consequence; mixed-up lists cost the marks.

medium.restatement: Less oxygen cargo forces the whole transport system to speed up.
medium.analogy: A fleet with stolen vans: the rest must run more trips, wearing the roads faster.
medium.examPointer: Use irreversible when describing carbon monoxide's binding — it is the specification's word.

modules.title: Bronchitis and Emphysema
sourceHeadings: Diseases of the gas exchange system linked to smoking
modules.opening: Tar stimulates the airways' mucus glands to enlarge and overproduce; the mucus pools, blocks the smallest bronchioles and invites infection, while the cilia that should sweep it out are damaged and stop beating. The smoker's cough is the manual workaround. Frequent infections then summon phagocytes whose elastase digests the alveoli's elastic fibres — the alveoli lose their spring, burst, and the exchange surface shrinks.
keyPoints: Tar enlarges goblet cells and mucus glands, producing excess mucus.
Damaged cilia cannot sweep the mucus away, so it pools and breeds infection.
The smoker's cough is the attempt to shift the mucus manually.
Phagocytes responding to infection release elastase that digests alveolar elastic fibres.
Burst alveoli shrink the exchange surface, leaving sufferers breathless.

low.restatement: Mucus pools because the sweepers are broken; then the alveoli's springs are cut.
low.analogy: A cleaning crew on strike while the mess grows — then demolition of the storage shelves.
low.examPointer: Link tar to mucus to infection to elastase to lost surface — the full disease chain.

medium.restatement: Broken sweepers, then broken springs — bronchitis then emphysema.
medium.analogy: A escalator whose brushes fail, then whose steps crack: passengers pile up, capacity vanishes.
medium.examPointer: Order the chain correctly in answers; chronology carries the logic marks.

glossary.definition: A chemical that raises the chance of cancer developing; tar is one.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: chronic bronchitis and emphysema occurring together.
The enzyme phagocytes release, digesting the elastic fibres of the alveoli.
The beating hairs that sweep mucus upwards out of healthy airways.
